meta.location: The Lamanite lands and the Nephite borders
principles: Two men preparing at the same time

world_behind.title: Amalickiah uses towers for propaganda
world_behind.text: Verse 1 says he appointed men to speak to the Lamanites from their towers against the Nephites. Alma 31:13 and 14 had the Zoramite Rameumptom used the same way, a raised stand for one voice at a time; Amalickiah is putting a religious form to political use.

world_behind.title: His captains are Zoramite dissenters
world_behind.text: Verse 5 makes Zoramite dissenters his chief captains because of what they knew about Nephite defenses. Alma 31:8 to 11 records that people leaving the church twenty years earlier, and Alma 43:4 and 44 has them already fighting on the Lamanite side. Their military value is the accumulated cost of that dissension.

world_behind.title: Mormon runs the two preparations side by side
world_behind.text: Verse 7 sets Amalickiah obtaining power by fraud against Moroni preparing the minds of the people. The comparison is the chapter's structure.

world_behind.title: The fortifications are described concretely
world_behind.text: Verse 8 gives small forts, banks of earth, and walls of stone around the cities and the borders. Alma 49:4 and 18 describe what a Lamanite army met when it arrived, and Alma 50:2 to 6 adds timbers, pickets and towers on top. Three chapters build one description of Nephite fortification.

world_behind.title: The Nephite rule of engagement is stated
world_behind.text: Verse 14 permits defense and forbids offense, with the blade reserved for an enemy or for staying alive.

world_behind.title: Mormon makes his strongest personal claim here
world_behind.text: Verse 17 stakes the shaking of hell itself on men resembling this one. He says nothing comparable about anyone else.

world_behind.title: He immediately shares the credit
world_behind.text: Verses 18 and 19 set Moroni beside Ammon and the sons of Mosiah, beside Alma and his sons, and rate Helaman and his brethren no less serviceable. Mosiah 27 and 28 carry the sons of Mosiah, Alma 5 through 16 carry Alma, and Alma 31 through 35 carry Helaman, so the verse works as an index to thirty chapters the reader has already been through.

words.text: Treated at Mosiah 11:12, of a tower Noah built. The phrase places of resort occurs three times in this record and never in the King James Bible, and here it names the fortified points a Zoramite captain would know how to find.

Treated at 2 Nephi 10:12. The related noun fortifications runs to ten uses here and none in the King James Bible, mostly across these war chapters. Verse 9 gives Moroni's principle: the most men at the weakest points.

Comprehension, judgment. Mormon calls Moroni a man of a perfect understanding, a phrase used once in this record and once in the King James Bible, where Luke claims it of his own research before writing his gospel (Luke 1:3).
Useful, of service. The word occurs once in scripture. Mormon uses it to say Helaman and his brethren were no less serviceable than Moroni, which is his way of ranking preaching level with defense.
Unwillingness. The word appears once in all of scripture. Mormon uses it of a people whose wars did not cease for many years, and he uses the adverb in verse 21 as well.

Savage, uncivilized. Its count is one here and one in the King James Bible, of the islanders who showed Paul kindness after the shipwreck. Mormon uses it of what dissenters would do to Nephite families.

phrases.term: He did appoint men to speak unto the Lamanites from their towers
phrases.text: The war opens with speeches. Amalickiah's first act as king is to organize a campaign of address, and verse 3 gives the result: hardened hearts, blinded minds, a numerous host.

phrases.term: They being the most acquainted with the strength of the Nephites
phrases.text: The value of a dissenter, stated plainly. Zoramite captains bring knowledge of the resorts and the weak points, which is why they get the commands.

phrases.term: While Amalickiah had thus been obtaining power by fraud and deceit, Moroni, on the other hand, had been preparing the minds of the people
phrases.text: Mormon's hinge sentence. The same months produced two kinds of preparation, and the rest of the chapter unfolds the second.

phrases.term: In their weakest fortifications he did place the greater number of men
phrases.text: Moroni's method in one line. The principle is that strength goes where the danger is, and Alma 49 shows the Lamanites arriving at exactly those points.

phrases.term: That which was called by their enemies the cause of Christians
phrases.text: Mormon repeats the point of Alma 46: the name came from outside. Here it names what the fortifications were built to protect.

phrases.term: A man that did not delight in bloodshed
phrases.text: The first thing Mormon says about Moroni's character after his strength. The whole portrait in verses 11 through 13 is built out of what he loved and what he had sworn.

phrases.term: Never to give an offense, yea, and never to raise the sword except it were against an enemy
phrases.text: The Nephite rule of engagement. Alma 43 quoted the Lord on the first and second offense; here Mormon gives it as standing instruction rather than as a ruling.

phrases.term: If all men had been, and were, and ever would be, like unto Moroni
phrases.text: Mormon's own claim, and the strongest he makes about any person in the record. He says the powers of hell would have been shaken forever.

phrases.term: He was a man like unto Ammon, the son of Mosiah
phrases.text: Mormon widens the praise immediately. The list runs through the sons of Mosiah, Alma and his sons, and verse 19 adds Helaman and his brethren as no less serviceable.

phrases.term: They were sorry to be the means of sending so many of their brethren out of this world
phrases.text: The reason for the reluctance, and it is theological. The Nephites are grieved at sending men to meet God unprepared, which is a concern about the enemy's standing rather than their own.

phrases.term: They could not suffer to lay down their lives, that their wives and their children should be massacred
phrases.text: The limit on the reluctance. Mormon states the sorrow first and the refusal second, and the two verses together are his account of why they fought at all.

verses.label: v. 8–9
verses.title: A defensive rule that runs against instinct
verses.text: The fortification programme is described by its materials, "erecting small forts, or places of resort; throwing up banks of earth round about to enclose his armies, and also building walls of stone," and then by a policy: "in their weakest fortifications he did place the greater number of men." The rule is counterintuitive and stated without argument. Numbers go where the works are poorest, which is a distribution decision rather than a construction one.

verses.label: v. 11–13
verses.title: One noun phrase, six times in three verses
verses.text: The portrait is built by repetition of a single construction: "a strong and a mighty man; he was a man of a perfect understanding; yea, a man that did not delight in bloodshed; a man whose soul did joy in the liberty and the freedom of his country"; then "a man whose heart did swell with thanksgiving to his God"; "a man who did labor exceedingly for the welfare and safety of his people." Six occurrences of a man in three verses, each introducing a different quality. The record gives no incident to illustrate any of them.

verses.label: v. 14
verses.title: The rule of engagement stated with its exceptions
verses.text: The doctrine is given as one sentence with three clauses, and the last two are limits on the first: the Nephites were taught "to defend themselves against their enemies, even to the shedding of blood if it were necessary; yea, and they were also taught never to give an offense, yea, and never to raise the sword except it were against an enemy, except it were to preserve their lives." Two exception clauses stack at the end, and the second narrows the first, so the permission is bounded twice inside a single verse.

verses.label: v. 17
verses.title: A superlative in three tenses at once
verses.text: The claim about the man is made conditional and then stretched across all time: "if all men had been, and were, and ever would be, like unto Moroni, behold, the very powers of hell would have been shaken forever." Past, present and future are stated in a row before the consequence arrives. It is the strongest thing the record says about any person, and it is put in a form that cannot be tested, since the condition it depends on has never held.

verses.label: v. 18–19
verses.title: The comparison extended, and then flatly equalised
verses.text: Having made the claim about one man, the record immediately widens it: "he was a man like unto Ammon, the son of Mosiah, yea, and even the other sons of Mosiah, yea, and also Alma and his sons, for they were all men of God." Verse 19 then refuses to rank the general above the preachers: "Helaman and his brethren were no less serviceable unto the people than was Moroni." A chapter that has spent nine verses praising a military commander declines, in its tenth, to say he mattered more than the men who preached.

verses.label: v. 21–25
verses.title: Reluctance stated four times in five verses
verses.text: The record will not let the war be read as willing. Verse 21: they "were compelled reluctantly to contend with their brethren." Verse 22: "their wars never did cease for the space of many years with the Lamanites, notwithstanding their much reluctance." Verse 23: "they were sorry to take up arms against the Lamanites, because they did not delight in the shedding of blood." Verse 24 gives the reason they fought anyway, "they could not suffer to lay down their lives, that their wives and their children should be massacred."

chapter.title: Two preparations, one sentence apart
chapter.text: Verse 7 puts Amalickiah's fraud and Moroni's teaching in the same clause. Mormon organizes the whole chapter as a comparison of how two men spent the same months.

chapter.title: The war opens with speeches on both sides
chapter.text: Verse 1 gives one method, "he did appoint men to speak unto the Lamanites from their towers, against the Nephites." Verse 7 gives the other in the same construction, "while Amalickiah had thus been obtaining power by fraud and deceit, Moroni, on the other hand, had been preparing the minds of the people to be faithful unto the Lord their God." Both verbs are about persuasion. Only at verse 8 does anything physical happen, and even that is defensive, "erecting small forts, or places of resort; throwing up banks of earth." The first three verses of the war are speeches.

chapter.title: The fortification principle is stated once and used repeatedly
chapter.text: Most men at the weakest points. Alma 49 through 52 are largely the working out of that sentence.

chapter.title: The character sketch is unusually long
chapter.text: Three verses of praise for a living man, in a record that rarely pauses for portraits. Mormon is establishing a standard he will measure others against.

chapter.title: Mormon's strongest claim is about a soldier
chapter.text: The powers of hell shaken forever. He then names five other men and a group of preachers in the next two verses, which keeps the claim from being about the office.

chapter.title: The rule forbids giving offense
chapter.text: Not merely starting wars. Verse 14 sets a standard on conduct that is stricter than the permission to fight.

chapter.title: The reluctance is given two grounds and one limit
chapter.text: They did not want blood, and they did not want men dying unprepared. What overrode both was what would happen to their families.

chapter.title: Four years of peace fit in one verse
chapter.text: Verse 20 covers them and verse 21 ends them. Mormon gives the whole war block its pace here: long stretches summarized, single days at length.

applications.title: Assume the defectors know your weak points
applications.text: Amalickiah made Zoramites his chief captains on the strength of what they knew about Nephite defenses from the inside. When someone leaves your side for the other one, the first question is what they carry with them, and the second is what you should change because they carry it.

applications.title: Prepare minds before you prepare defenses
applications.text: Mormon lists Moroni's teaching before his walls. When something difficult is coming, the first work is on what people understand and expect.

applications.title: Put your strength where you are weakest
applications.text: Moroni reinforced the poorest fortifications. Identify the part of your life or work that would fail first, and put resources there rather than into what is already strong.

applications.title: Settle the limit before the pressure arrives
applications.text: Moroni had already sworn his oath of defense, so the commitment was fixed before any war came to test it. Draw your line while you are calm, because a line drawn during the crisis bends to the crisis.

applications.title: Say what you will not do
applications.text: Never give offense, never raise the sword except against an enemy. Write down the things you will not do in a conflict, before you are in one.

applications.title: Count the quiet work as equal
applications.text: Mormon rates Helaman and his brethren no less serviceable than Moroni, giving the preachers the same standing as the general. When you tally who carried a hard season, include the people whose contribution left no visible marks.

applications.title: Let the reluctance stay
applications.text: The Nephites fought and remained sorry about it. When you have to do something hard and justified, you do not have to stop regretting that it was necessary.

applications.title: Say what the refusal would cost
applications.text: The reason given for fighting is what would have happened to wives and children if they had not. When you weigh whether to act, spell out the consequence of standing still with the same care you gave the consequence of moving.

questions.text: Who is speaking to me daily, and what are they for?
What does someone who left know about my weak points?
What have I been preparing while somebody else prepared something else?
If someone described my character in three sentences, what would be first?
What offense have I given without thinking of it as one?
What would be true of the world if everyone were like me?
What have I done that was right and still grieved me?
